newsitem.title: LEBANON: Lebanon belatedly cuts pound lending rates.
newsitem.headline: Lebanon belatedly cuts pound lending rates.

text.p: The Lebanese Banks Association said on Thursday it had slashed the Lebanese pound prime lending rate to 18 percent from 24 percent following cuts in treasury bill yields.

The association, grouping 79 of Lebanon's 82 banks, said in a statement that the rate cut was decided by its board on Tuesday. The last cut was in January 1996, when the prime rate was reduced to 24 percent from 30 percent.
Makram Sader, the association's secretary-general, said the cut was in line with a fall in pound-denominated treasury bill yields and was also aimed at boosting lending in the local currency.

"There are two reasons behind cutting the prime rate, the first is the trend of falling treasury bill rates and the second is boosting lending in Lebanese pounds, which is very important," Sader told Reuters.

"This is a lagging not a leading indicator which merely reflects the gradual and much-anticipated drop in interest rates we have been witnessing since the beginning of November," Nabil Chaya, Banque Audi's Lebanese pound treasurer, told Reuters.
"I wonder why the Lebanese Banks Association dropped the prime rate six points and not gradually in line with the yield drops on t-bills?" Chaya said.
"Institutional investors from abroad are calling and wondering about this massive six-point cut."
Asked to comment, Sader said that although the banks association had wanted to cut the prime rate by stages last year, it could not do so on a weekly basis in the same way as t-bill auctions.

Another reason for the delay was a 17-day Israeli blitz last April after which two-year t-bill yields -- to which the prime rate in Lebanon is more closely linked than other yields -- remained relatively high.
"The prime rate should have gone down to 21 or 20 percent last April but we had the April incidents and two-year t-bill yields remained relatively high," Sader said.
Lebanese t-bills of three-month, six-month, one-year and two-year maturities currently yield 14.21 percent, 16.01 percent, 16.76 percent and 18.70 percent respectively.
They were 14.61 percent, 16.92 percent, 17.78 percent and 21.62 percent three months ago.
One Beirut banker said the rate cut would boost pound lending a little but further reductions were needed to bring it in line with lower dollar lending rates of 10-14 percent.
The dollar prime rate for Lebanon's major commercial banks remains 10.5 percent, according to the association.

Another banker said the prime rate cut would encourage the Lebanese to borrow more in their local currency but a further cut was needed as people still prefer to borrow in dollars because of lower rates.
"When it (the prime rate) goes down to say 15 percent, then it becomes reasonable as that would be close to the dollar rates," said the banker, who asked not to be identified.
The association also urged banks to lower the pound credit rate for three-month, six-month, one-year and two-year time deposits to less than the corresponding t-bill yields.
The banker said he doubted banks would strictly stick to lower credit rates "as there is competition between them".
